 Retired Chinese gymnast Lu Yufei recovers $22,500 in overdue social security payments after speaking out online
 By Hoang Nguyen    November 20, 2026 | 08:00 pm PT 
 Get VnExpress first in Google Search 
 See more of the news you trust. Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results
 Lu Yufei, a retired Chinese national gymnast, has recovered nearly 150,000 yuan ($22,500) in overdue social security back payments after voicing the issue online, prompting local authorities and her former employer to settle 91 months of missed contributions. 
 Chinese gymnast Lu Yufei competing in the uneven bars in the women’s all-around final at the Tokyo Olympic Games in 2021. Photo by AFP
 In China, mandatory social security is viewed as a second salary rather than an optional perk. When Lu, 26, posted her plea for help on Weibo, it rapidly surged to the top of trending searches on Wednesday afternoon.
 "I only found out after retiring that my former employer hadn’t paid my social security and pension insurance," Lu wrote, as quoted by the South China Morning Post . "What should I do in this situation? Has anyone experienced the same thing? I’d like to ask everyone what to do about these 10 years of social security and 15 years of service."
 Alongside her message, she attached a screenshot of her personal basic pension insurance statement for government and public institution employees in Henan Province.
 The record indicated that Lu began working on Jan. 1, 2011, and enrolled in the scheme on Sept. 1, 2016. However, her payment status was listed as "suspended (interrupted)" with 91 months in arrears.
 The unpaid principal totaled 149,946.56 yuan, broken down into 102,260.32 yuan owed by her employer and 47,686.24 yuan of her personal share.
 Under China's Social Insurance Law, contributions are mandatory. Employers are required to register staff within 30 days and make full, timely payments covering pension, medical, unemployment, work-related injury and maternity insurance.
 This safety net is designed to protect citizens during old age, illness, or unemployment, and serves as the sole baseline protection for elite athletes forced into early retirement by sports injuries. Months of missed payments not only jeopardized Lu’s future pension eligibility, but also meant portions previously deducted from her wages had never been properly paid.
 By Wednesday evening, she shared an update confirming that authorities had intervened to address the dispute, asking the public to "view the matter rationally, avoid over-amplifying public opinion and patiently await the follow-up results."
 On Thursday morning, Lu announced that the issue had been "properly resolved."
 "After the incident gained traction, relevant authorities and my former employer quickly took it seriously, communicated with me continuously last night, and completed paying all the unpaid contributions," Lu wrote.
 She also apologized for occupying public attention, emphasizing that the matter concerned only her own rights and "does not represent the entire industry," while urging followers to continue supporting Chinese sports.
 Born in Zhengzhou, Henan, Lu was recruited by the Henan gymnastics team in 2011 at just 10 years old and earned a spot on the national team in 2014.
 She captured one gold, one silver and two bronze medals at the National Youth Games in 2015, before winning gold in the women’s team and asymmetric bars, alongside all-around silver, at the 2019 Asian Gymnastics Championships.
 In 2021, Lu claimed all-around and floor exercise titles at the National Gymnastics Championships, finished fourth in both the women’s team and uneven bars at the Tokyo Olympics, and secured uneven bars silver at the National Games in Xi'an, earning Henan's first-ever National Games medal in women’s gymnastics.
 After gradually stepping back from elite competition due to injuries, Lu retired to become a gymnastics judge and has since amassed more than one million followers across social media.
